to.text: The FOMC raises the federal funds target range by 25 basis points, to 4.00%-4.25%, at the meeting ending December 9, 2026.

to.title: The Fed raises by a half point or more on December 9
to.text: The FOMC raises the federal funds target range by 50 basis points or more, to 4.25%-4.50% or higher, at the meeting ending December 9, 2026. Governor Waller is the only official to back it publicly; New York Fed President Williams has ruled it out.

shock.note: A half-point move against 6-7% priced would lift front-end yields by roughly 15-20bp and signal a faster path. On Nov 10, 2026, when hot CPI moved the 2-year 17bp, the S&P 500 lost 0.4% in a day; a surprise at the meeting itself, with Waller's 'shock' framing, is larger. I put the S&P 1.5% below where a quarter point leaves it.
On Nov 10 the 10-year rose 10bp for a 17bp move in the 2-year (CNN, 'Bond yields surge most in 19 months'); hawkish Fed news this month has flattened the curve, so I carry about 6bp to the long end.
A wider rate gap extends the dollar's rally; the dollar index is already at a 19-month high on hike expectations, so the further move is modest.
BND's duration is near 6 and its yields sit in the 2- to 10-year part of the curve, which moves more than the long end on a policy surprise: about 12bp there is -0.7%.

A hold, priced at about 3%, removes roughly 15bp from front-end yields. Relief for equities is tempered because a Fed that holds with core inflation running 3.5-3.7% annualised invites doubt about inflation control. I put the S&P 0.8% above the quarter-point baseline.
Lower policy-rate expectations pull long yields down while a larger inflation-risk premium pushes them up; I take the two to cancel at the long end.
The dollar's 19-month high rests on hike expectations; a hold takes some of that back.
Intermediate yields fall about 7bp on a hold; with duration near 6 that is +0.4%.

fields.title: The Fed's rate is 4.75% or higher after its April 28, 2027 meeting
fields.text: The upper bound of the federal funds target range stands at 4.75% or higher after the FOMC meeting that ends April 28, 2027: at least three more quarter-point rises from today's 3.75%-4.00% across the December, January, March and April meetings. April's is the last meeting inside the horizon.

chances.note: If the Fed raises in December, January and March the rate is already 4.75% after March; it stays at or above that unless April brings a cut. Polymarket's April-decision market puts a cut at about 12% unconditionally, and a cut one meeting after three straight rises is less likely than that, so 0.92.

Without three straight rises, 4.75% by April needs two rises by March and another in April, or a half-point step. Polymarket's parlay puts two-of-three paths (Hike-Hike-Pause, Hike-Pause-Hike) at about 0.53 of all paths, 0.80 of the paths that are not Hike-Hike-Hike; an April rise is priced near 0.24. 0.80 x 0.24 is 0.19.

shock.note: The Fed stopping after December (or reversing) by April has two causes with opposite effects on stocks: inflation cooling fast as oil falls (S&P up a few percent), or growth and markets cracking (S&P down around 10%). Kalshi prices a cut before July 2027 near 45%, which says the second is live. I weight them about evenly and put the S&P 1% below the baseline; the sign is the least certain figure in this row.
Long yields fall in both versions: about 0.15 points if inflation cools, more if growth cracks. The reverse of the +0.12 points seen when one extra rise was priced, scaled up for the stress case.
The dollar's 19-month high rests on the rate gap; a Fed that stops gives back about what it gained when one rise was priced.
The mirror of BND's 1.7% fall when one extra rise was priced: one or more rises fewer than the baseline.

chances.note: Polymarket asks this downturn by December 31, 2026 and by June 30, 2027 on identical rules (three of six triggers inside 90 days). May 18 falls between; I read the date at a constant daily hazard between the two deadlines, since no scheduled date concentrates the risk.

shock.note: The market's triggers need the semiconductor index 40% below its record; SMH is about 26% below its October peak today. A world that meets the trigger has chip stocks roughly 20% under today's level, which against a no-downturn world slightly above today is about -23%. The fall already seen from Oct 30 to Nov 18 (SMH -12%) is the same move at smaller scale.

Since the October record the S&P has lost about 8% while chip stocks lost about 26%, a ratio near 0.3. A further 20% in chips on that ratio is 6-7%; a recognised bust adds the unwind of AI financing (Nvidia disclosed $118 billion of maximum guarantee exposure) and of the capex that has been carrying growth, so I put the S&P 11% below the no-downturn world.

An AI bust is a growth shock: the Fed's remaining rises come out of the curve and money moves to Treasuries. Long yields fell about 5bp over the last four sessions of the chip selloff even with hikes being priced; a full bust is worth about a quarter point.

The trigger needs Nvidia 50% below its record. It is about 35% below now (J.P. Morgan study cited by Benzinga, Nov 18), so the trigger price is near $116 against $147 today; worlds that cross it sit a little under it on average, about 25% below today, which is 28.5% below the no-downturn world.

Apple has been where money went in this AI selloff: +6.7% from Oct 1 to Nov 18 while Nvidia lost 35% and the S&P 4.5% (window). It would not rise through an 11% fall in the index, but it falls about half as far.

from.text: China commences a military offensive intended to establish control over any portion of the main island of Taiwan by June 30, 2027, as Polymarket's market defines it.
from.resolution_source: Polymarket 'Will China invade Taiwan by June 30, 2027?' rules; consensus of credible reporting

taken.note: A longshot contract held to mid-2027: at 4.2 cents the price is consistent with a risk-neutral probability anywhere from about 1.5% to 4.3% once the cost of tying up money is counted, and such contracts carry lottery demand on the Yes side. Its book is $204 deep. I read it as an upper bound and state my own figure, which follows it.

chances.note: My figure for an invasion by mid-2027 is 2.5% against the market's 4.2%: the lower part of the range its price allows, weighted up from 1.5% because 2027 is the PLA's stated readiness year and Xi raised Taiwan directly with Trump this week. It moves in proportion with the market's odds.

shock.note: Bloomberg Economics puts a blockade short of invasion at 5.3% of global GDP, with chip inventories gone within weeks. The April 2025 tariff shock, a trade disruption far smaller than cutting off the island that makes most advanced chips, took the S&P down 12% in four sessions (window). I put a blockade-or-attack world 17% below the baseline, weighted toward blockade, with invasion worse.

Uncertain in sign. War risk pulls money into Treasuries, but in the April 2025 trade shock long yields rose 0.23 points (window), and a chip shortage is inflationary while China holds a large Treasury position. I take a small net fall.
The dollar gains against Asian currencies in a conflict centred on Taiwan; against the euro and yen the sign is less clear, so the index move is small.

TSMC's fabs, and the ports its output leaves through, are on the island. Under a blockade its revenue stops while the assets survive; under attack the assets are at risk. Half its value against the baseline is a blockade-weighted figure.

Apple fell 23% in the April 2025 tariff shock (window), which only taxed its China supply chain. A Taiwan blockade removes the processors for every iPhone and Mac and puts its China assembly and China sales inside the conflict.
Nvidia's chips are made and packaged at TSMC in Taiwan; it has no second source at scale. I put it slightly worse than the chip sector.
Toyota fell 10% in the April 2025 tariff shock (window). Japan sits beside the conflict, its shipping lanes run past Taiwan, and automakers stop for want of chips as in 2021.
VXUS fell 11% in the April 2025 tariff shock (window). Taiwan, China, Japan and Korea are about a third of the fund, and they are the markets a blockade hits first.

value.title: The US launches another round of extensive strikes on Iran by May 18, 2027
value.text: By May 18, 2027 the United States carries out a new round of extensive strikes on Iran, of the kind the New York Times and Israel's Channel 12 report Trump is weighing (nuclear facilities, infrastructure, senior officials), as opposed to the limited strikes that have continued through November such as those on Qeshm island. chances.note: If the US goes 14 days without striking Iran starting by Dec 31 (Polymarket puts that near 0.71), the low-level exchange has cooled and Trump's Nov 8 line holds: restarting the war is 'highly unlikely' if talks produce a strong agreement. Ceasefires in April and June both broke down within weeks, so a pause still leaves about one chance in five of an extensive round by May.

If US strikes continue through December with no 14-day pause, the flare-up Rabobank describes ('ships are still being attacked and President Trump is yet again considering plans for another round of extensive strikes') has not cooled, and Israel is pressing for action against Iran's rebuilt missile stock. An extensive round by May is then about even.

passages: Global benchmark Brent has retreated by more than a fifth so far this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and Trump held off on renewed large-scale strikes against the Islamic Republic. Still, there’s been a flare-up in low-level fighting across the region in recent days, including a spate of attacks on vessels transiting the critical Strait of Hormuz.

“We are not yet at the point where the narrative of improving supply is enough to overshadow the military flare-ups in the region,” said Florence Schmit, a senior energy strategist at Rabobank. “Flows through Hormuz have improved, yet ships are still being attacked and President Trump is yet again considering plans for another round of extensive strikes on Iran.”

to.text: By May 18, 2027 the United States and Iran agree a nuclear deal that limits Iran's programme in exchange for sanctions relief, without a new round of extensive US strikes before it.
to.resolution_source: US and Iranian government statements; consensus of major news reporting

chances.note: Kalshi asks a deal before July 1, 2027. May 18 is 180 of the 224 days to that deadline, and Kalshi's own ladder puts 0.095 of its 0.205 before March 1, so about three quarters of deals by July land by May 18; of those, I take 0.85 to come without an extensive round of strikes first. 0.75 x 0.85 is about 0.62.

shock.note: A deal brings sanctions relief for Iranian barrels and ends the threat to Hormuz. Crude already fell 19% from Oct 30 to Nov 18 as Gulf supply recovered (window) and Saxo notes 'renewing concerns about an emerging supply glut'; a signed deal takes Brent from about $92 toward the high $70s, 15% below the standoff.

Energy costs are driving inflation here and abroad (euro-area 4.0%, 'with energy costs driving both'), and that inflation is why the Fed is raising rates. Cheaper oil eases both; I put the S&P 2% above the standoff.
Lower oil takes some inflation premium out of long yields: about a third of the 0.22-point rise seen when the war began (window), in reverse.

Exxon fell 13.8% while crude fell 19% from Oct 30 to Nov 18 (window), about 0.7 of oil's move. For a further 15% in oil I use 8%, a little over half, since part of the war premium has already left the shares.

Brent 'has retreated by more than a fifth so far this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and Trump held off on renewed large-scale strikes'. An extensive round reverses that: Iran has warned neighbours of retaliation and ships in Hormuz are already under attack. The first month of the war lifted crude 61% (window); with Gulf flows now partly rerouted and the market practised, I use 22%, roughly back to late October's level.

fields.text: The United States and China do not agree or announce a further extension of the Busan trade truce before January 11, 2027, so China's suspended additional 24% tariff on US goods and the suspended US port fees on China-linked ships come back into force. Beijing has threatened countermeasures to the new US rule on overseas access to AI chips.

shock.note: On Oct 10, 2025, when the same truce came under threat (rare-earth controls answered by a 100% tariff threat), the S&P fell 2.7% in a day (window). A lapse is a break carried out, not threatened, but the measures that return are narrower than that threat; I use 3.5%.

Chip stocks fell 5.8% on Oct 10, 2025 (window). This time the dispute is about chips: China 'could retaliate with tighter rare earth export controls if Washington further restricts chip sales' (SCMP, Nov 13), and TSMC and Samsung have already suspended some shipments to Chinese customers.
Long yields fell 0.11 points on Oct 10, 2025 as money moved to Treasuries (window).

Apple fell 3.5% on Oct 10, 2025 (window) and 23% in the April 2025 tariff shock. It assembles most iPhones in China and sells about a sixth of its revenue there; near a record high it has room to fall, so 5%.
Toyota fell 3.7% on Oct 10, 2025 (window); automakers depend on Chinese rare-earth magnets.
VXUS fell 2.3% on Oct 10, 2025 (window); its Chinese and other Asian holdings are the direct casualties.

fields.title: Apple guides its March-quarter gross margin below 45% on January 28
fields.text: At its fiscal first-quarter report, projected for January 28, 2027, Apple guides gross margin for the March quarter with a midpoint below 45.0%: a second step down after the 45%-46% it guided for the December quarter, against 47.9% reported for September.
fields.resolution_source: Apple fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call and release

chances.note: Management warned 'that memory costs could rise beyond the December quarter, while supply constraints may affect Mac and iPad into next year', and September's 47.9% carried about a point of tariff refunds that will not repeat. Against that, the March quarter leans more to Services, Apple raised iPhone prices by about $100, and it has 'longer-term memory contracts'. A further step below 45% is somewhat less likely than holding the 45%-46% range: one chance in three.

passages: The pressure point is the coming quarter. Apple expects a 45% to 46% gross margin, compared with 47.9% in the quarter just reported. Gross margin is the share of sales left after direct product and service costs, before other business expenses.

Higher memory-chip and AI costs are part of the squeeze. The comparison also includes a benefit that will not necessarily repeat: tariff refunds lifted the reported quarter’s margin by about one percentage point.
At the same time, investors continue to weigh management’s warning that memory costs could rise beyond the December quarter, while supply constraints may affect Mac and iPad into next year.

shock.note: Bulls already 'brushed off near-term memory margin headwinds' and the shares sit near a record, so proof that margins have turned adds less than a further fall would take away: 3% beyond what the shares would otherwise do.

The first step down in margin guidance cost 1.9% the next day (to $331.90 on Nov 3) before the shares rallied with the market. They now trade near a record after gaining 12% beyond the factors since Oct 1 (window), with KeyBanc calling them 'at the point of extreme overvaluation' and short interest up 10%. A second step down, showing the squeeze is not one quarter long, is worth about 5% beyond what the shares would otherwise do.

fields.title: Microsoft's Azure growth falls below 48% in its January 27 report
fields.text: At its fiscal second-quarter report, projected for January 27, 2027, Microsoft reports constant-currency growth in Azure and other cloud services below 48% for the December quarter: the acceleration from 48% in the September quarter stalls or reverses.

chances.note: Azure beat its own guidance by three to four points last quarter (48% against 44%-45%), and analysts look for 49%-50%. A print under 48% needs that pattern to break. What could break it: capacity ('capacity constraints prevented Azure from growing even faster'), this month's outages, and capital spending that already came in below expectations. I put it a little above one in five.

passages: Slowinski highlighted 48% constant-currency Azure growth in the fiscal first quarter, above management’s 44%-45% guidance, while Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud grew 18%.
He expects Azure growth to accelerate further to 49%-50% in the fiscal second quarter and Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud growth to reach 19%.
Munster also said capacity constraints prevented Azure from growing even faster, reinforcing Microsoft’s need for additional infrastructure investment.

to.title: Azure growth accelerates above 50%
to.text: Microsoft reports constant-currency Azure growth above 50.0% for the December quarter at its January 27, 2027 report.

chances.note: Another beat of the size of last quarter's against a 49%-50% expectation puts growth above 50%. Microsoft has beaten its Azure guidance in recent quarters, but capacity is the limit management cites, so I put this a little above one in four.

shock.note: Microsoft has fallen from $554 on Nov 4 to $500 as outages and the software selloff hit it. A clear acceleration answers Dan Ives's 'six-month window' for AI to show monetisation; the shares rose about 6% on Nov 4 when investors rotated back to it. 5% beyond what the shares would otherwise do.

Azure's acceleration is the reason analysts hold targets of $610-$722 with free cash flow set to turn negative in the second half of the fiscal year on capital spending. A stall would put the spending without the growth; Alphabet lost 11.8% in a day on Oct 29 for a capex-heavy quarter with negative free cash flow. I use 7% beyond what Microsoft would otherwise do.

fields.title: Nvidia cuts its fiscal-2028 growth outlook on February 24
fields.text: At its fiscal fourth-quarter report, projected for February 24, 2027, Nvidia lowers its outlook for fiscal-2028 revenue growth below the roughly 75% it gave on November 17, 2026, or withdraws it.
fields.resolution_source: Nvidia fiscal Q4 2027 earnings release and call

chances.note: Nvidia raised this outlook to 75% from 70% a week ago with demand ahead of supply, so a cut within one quarter needs something to change. Three things can: the 90-day licence deadline for overseas data centres serving Chinese customers falls about ten days before the report, on sales Luria puts at 5% to 20% of the total; customer financing ('access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear' if Nvidia stops guaranteeing, per Apollo's Rowan), with the $500 billion plan yet to fund a deal; and an interim or newly arrived CEO resetting the bar. One in five.

passages: After NVIDIA’s quarterly report, Luria said demand remained strong enough for the company to raise its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to 75% from 70%, even as it acknowledged uncertainty around Asian sales.

Luria estimates that 5% to 20% of NVIDIA chip sales may have reached China directly or through resellers and Asian data centers, which drove his price-target reduction to \$200 from \$300, despite maintaining a Buy rating.

Data centers that already serve those customers have 90 days to obtain a license. Operators are also expected to check who ultimately owns their clients, and a customer that refuses to answer is treated as a red flag.

On Tuesday’s [Nvidia earnings call](https://www.benzinga.com/content/63374236/nvidia-q3-2027-earnings-call-transcript), Kress said the company would be selective about the deals it backs. Apollo CEO **Marc Rowan** told CNBC that if Nvidia stopped acting as guarantor, "access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear." Those companies buy chips and rent out the computing power.

chances.note: It raised the figure last quarter and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion against about $125 billion expected, with the Vera Rubin ramp its fastest. A second raise in a row is plausible but less likely than holding while the export and financing questions are open: three in ten.

shock.note: The November beat-and-raise did not lift the shares: they fell 5.2% beyond the factors from Nov 11 to Nov 18 (window) because leadership and export questions dominated. A second raise helps more if those have eased by February; I allow 5% beyond what the shares would otherwise do.
Nvidia is about 22% of TSMC's 2026 sales; a higher Nvidia outlook is a higher order book for TSMC.

The 75% outlook is what holds analysts' targets (Luria cut his to $200 from $300 on the China question alone and kept a Buy). The shares are already down 35% since Oct 1 (window) with ten bank downgrades; a cut would confirm the bear case that sales rested on China-linked buyers and on Nvidia's own financing. 12% beyond what the shares would otherwise do.
TSMC lost 4.2% beyond the factors from Nov 11 to Nov 18 on doubts about Nvidia's orders alone (window); a cut to Nvidia's outlook makes the doubt a fact for its largest customer.

Nvidia is the largest weight in the chip sector and its outlook is the sector's demand signal; memory, equipment and networking names fell 7-8% on Nov 16 on export news about Nvidia's customers. 3% for the sector beyond the market.

(4) AI regulation from the incoming Democratic Congress: the Nov 5 fall (Nasdaq -5.5%) priced the fear; with a presidential veto, law inside the horizon is unlikely, and the AI-downturn row carries the consequence if the build-out slows. (5) The run of outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan, Apple and the FAA: officials deny a coordinated attack; I found no way to put a probability on a systemic cyber event and no market that asks it. (6) A generic 'bear market' row: an index level is where the events above would show, not an event of its own, so I removed it. (7) Novo's 2027 guidance in February is a second Novo catalyst beside the CagriSema decision; I did not find a consensus figure to define it against.

items.text:
Your $504k account is about three-quarters stocks, 17% bonds, 2.4% bitcoin and the rest cash. After looking through the funds, 14.6% sits in chip stocks, with Apple at 8.3%, Microsoft at 6.9% and Nvidia at 6.7%. Over the six months to May 18, ordinary market movement alone is about ±$42,700. I built 13 events on top of that; each row is read alone, so they do not add.

**The AI build-out and Taiwan are the two largest risks**
- **AI downturn:** prop:2 is the biggest row. The Forecast is about 17%, read from Polymarket's two deadlines, and Yes costs about $36,700 (7.3%). The assumption driving it is that the S&P stands 11% lower in a recognised bust; chip stocks are already about 26% below their October peak.
- **Taiwan:** prop:4 is unlikely at about 3.6% but costs about $82,000 (16%), because TSMC, Nvidia and Apple all depend on the island. I set the Forecast below Polymarket's invasion price, which I read as an upper bound.
- **Nvidia itself:** prop:29 is the dated test after Jensen Huang's resignation; a cut costs about $4,900 and a raise adds about $2,600. prop:3 is the upside, worth about $2,300.

**Rates hit your stocks and bonds together**
- **Fed path:** prop:12 is close to a coin flip. The Worst outcome is a rate of 5% or higher (11.5%), costing about $18,200. Your bond funds do not cushion this one.
- **December meeting:** prop:1 is nearly settled; only a half-point rise (6%, about −$6,600) or a hold (3%, about +$4,300) would move you.

**Geopolitics and trade**
- **Iran:** prop:5 costs about $8,900 on Yes, with Exxon offsetting only part. A nuclear deal (about 13%) is the favourable outcome, worth about +$9,700 through cheaper oil. The 30% Forecast is my own judgement, tied to a Polymarket ceasefire contract; no market asks it directly.
- **China trade:** prop:21 costs about $11,800 on Yes; its Forecast comes from a thin Kalshi book.

**Smaller, dated rows**
- **Apple:** prop:23 is my estimate from management's warning on memory costs; about −$1,700 on Yes.
- **Microsoft:** prop:26 is also my estimate; about −$2,400 on Yes, about +$1,800 if growth tops 50%.
- **Bitcoin:** prop:7 is about ±$3,200 either way, of which roughly $2,400 is the bitcoin fund itself.
- **Novo Nordisk:** prop:6 is expected; a rejection costs about $1,200.
- **Shutdown:** prop:8 is likely to make noise but costs only about $1,300; the 43-day shutdown in 2025 did not hurt markets.

**Reading them together**
Read together, prop:2, prop:12 and prop:4 give a Volatility of about ±$21,900. In the calm case, where none of them goes wrong and the Fed stops at 4.50% (31%), you gain about $16,900. I stated three dependencies for that reading: a bust makes further Fed rises less likely, makes an Nvidia cut more likely, and a Taiwan blockade would itself trigger the bust.

**Where I am least sure**
- The sign of the stock move if the Fed stops early: it could mean cooling inflation or a cracking economy.
- Long Treasury yields in a Taiwan crisis: they rose in the April 2025 trade shock.
- The size of the S&P fall in an AI bust.

note:87 lists what I left out and why, including JPMorgan, Toyota and the yen, a Ukraine settlement, AI regulation and the recent outages.
